newsitem.title: GERMANY: Lufthansa says won't change offer to union.
newsitem.headline: Lufthansa says won't change offer to union.

text.p: Lufthansa AG, hardening its stance a day before the results of a strike ballot by pilots and flight attendants will be released, said on Tuesday it would not change the pay offer the union has already rejected.

The German airline said the "overwhelming majority" of its 58,000 workers were against a walkout by pilots and flight attendants who are members of the DAG union. The airline added that "clearly less than 10 percent" of its workforce was in the union.

Lufthansa said its offer of new talks with the DAG was still on the table but that it saw little room to manoeuvre from the deal it signed in October 1996 with the OeTV union that represents ground personnel at the airline.

The DAG union plans on Wednesday to release the results of the balloting that would give union leaders the right to call a strike. DAG members must give at least 70 percent approval to the ballot, a level the union has said would be met.
The DAG has said a strike would only be called if attempts at talks with Lufthansa management were to fail but has said it would not return to talks unless a new offer was made.

"The current conflict is, among other things, being led by workers who are among the better wage-earners at the company but also work in an area where 170 new jobs were created last year," the airline said in a statement.
Pilots and flight attendants are opposed to the OeTV deal, which Lufthansa reached with the union after talks with the DAG had broken off last autumn.

The 27-month contract agreed to by the OeTV calls for Lufthansa workers to receive a one-off payment equal to one-third of a month's base pay, a 1.7 percent raise in 1998 and a small bonus in cash or Lufthansa stock.

The DAG has demanded a higher wage offer and wants only a one-year deal, the top priority for the union reluctant to get locked into a multi-year contract as the airline seeks to cut costs to improve its competitive stance when European skies are opened in April.
Lufthansa's statement was the latest effort to isolate DAG members, which staged staged two brief warning strikes in November and December that cost Lufthansa 30 million marks ($18 million).

The airline said an internal employee survey showed growing concerns about a strike at a time of record German jobless, including one worker it quoted as saying, "Be happy that you have a job. We already have 4.5 million unemployed" in Germany.

Lufthansa, which has said the impact of a strike on its future could be "fatal", also accused the DAG of spreading misinformation about cost-cutting measures aimed at trimming costs by as much as 20 percent to meet growing competition.
Flight attendants and pilots have expressed concern about Lufthansa's plans to hand over some routes to partner airlines signed up under the "Team Lufthansa" concept at lower wages.
The problem is similar to what prompted pilots at American Airlines, a unit of AMR Corp, to strike earlier this month before President Bill Clinton ordered them back to work.
But Lufthansa chief executive Juergen Weber cannot turn to Bonn for help -- German law prohibits the government from intervening in a collective-bargaining wage dispute.
DAG officials, saying their members would not bear the brunt of the downsizing, have long said they would not return to talks unless Lufthansa management put foward a new proposal.
The airline is under severe pressure to reduce its cost base, along with the high costs of German labour. ($ = 1.674 German Marks)
